extracted.intended_audience: general readers of 19th-century literary essays / readers interested in social commentary, poetry, and humorous reflection
extracted.subtask_description: Humorous, didactic literary-essay chapter mixing social observation, maxims, and reflections on exercise, aging, poetry, and manners (from Holmes' Autocrat of the Breakfast-Table).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading-aloud guidance (omit verses for average audiences)
rubrics_metrics.description: In reading aloud, omit, if you please, the sixth and seventh verses. These are parenthetical and digressive, and, unless your audience is of superior intelligence, will confuse them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor readings to your audience's capacity: remove parenthetical/digressive material (specifically verses 6 and 7 here) when addressing a general or less sophisticated audience to avoid confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive parenthesis when addressing listeners
rubrics_metrics.description: One has to dismount from an idea, and get into the saddle again, at every parenthesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parenthetical remarks interrupt flow and require effort to return to the main idea; minimize them when speaking or when you want to keep audience engagement and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hat as social signifier (axioms of dress and respectability)
rubrics_metrics.description: A hat which has been popped, or exploded by being sat down upon, is never itself again afterwards. Shabby gentility has nothing so characteristic as its hat. The last effort of decayed fortune is expended in smoothing its dilapidated castor. The hat is the ultimum moriens of 'respectability.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the hat (or analogous outward tokens) as an indicator of social standing in characterization or social commentary; note that damage or worn appearance signals irrecoverable social decline and is a reliable cue to readers/listeners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of pleasure in exercise
rubrics_metrics.description: The pleasure of exercise is due first to a purely physical impression, and secondly to a sense of power in action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing or prescribing exercise (or analogous activities), account for both immediate sensory/physical pleasures and the psychological feeling of agency/power; different audiences will value these sources differently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three powers in active exercise and their predominance
rubrics_metrics.description: In all forms of active exercise there are three powers simultaneously in action,—the will, the muscles, and the intellect. Each of these predominates in different kinds of exercise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify activities by which of the three predominates: walking frees the intellect (will and muscles are automatic), riding extends the will into another animal (satisfying tyrannical/heroic instincts), rowing maximally extends volition and muscular existence; use this framework to evaluate or recommend exercises according to desired mental/physical effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rowing: nearest approach to flying; efficiency of muscle labor
rubrics_metrics.description: This, in sober earnest, is the nearest approach to flying that man has ever made... It has been long agreed that there is no way in which a man can accomplish so much labor with his muscles as in rowing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray rowing as both liberating and highly efficient physical exertion; note the dual possibility of gentle, all-day rowing (allowing mental work) or brief intense exertion (to warm up quickly) when recommending or describing the activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical/manual work as relief for intellectual fatigue
rubrics_metrics.description: Some mechanical employment is the greatest possible relief, after the purely intellectual faculties begin to tire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocate hands-on, mechanical tasks (carpentry, carving) as restorative diversions for writers, thinkers, or anyone overtaxed by mental work; include concrete examples (carving a wooden toy) to show therapeutic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical grounding/profession for literary men
rubrics_metrics.description: The higher a man has to carry the raw material of thought before he works it up, the more it costs him in blood, nerve, and muscle. Coleridge knew all this very well when he advised every literary man to have a profession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend that writers maintain a profession or practical occupation to reduce the 'cost' of producing literary work and to provide steadiness and resources; use the metaphor of carrying raw material to illustrate cognitive/physiological burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety in poetic mood and style (pull more stops)
rubrics_metrics.description: A healthy mind ought to change its mood from time to time... 'The more stops, the better.' Poets commonly have no larger stock of tunes than hand-organs; the more stops, the better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advise poets and writers to vary tone, subject, and style regularly to avoid monotony or exhaustion of creative resources; use musical/hand-organ metaphor to justify deliberate diversification of 'stops' or modes.

rubrics_metrics.name: On the source of poetic inspiration and praise (role of women)
rubrics_metrics.description: Women. Their love first inspires the poet, and their praise is his best reward. I don't think they are the first to see one's defects, but they are the first to catch the color and fragrance of a true poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the emotional response and encouragement of close readers (here, women) as primary stimulants for poetic creation and validation; when discussing influences on creative work, acknowledge affective/audience responses as important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of poets: two kinds (constructive vs sensitive)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two kinds of poets... negative or washed blondes (sensitive, lacking coloring) and positive or stained blondes (sun-kindled, constructive imaginations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this typology to evaluate poets' temperaments and likely careers: the more sensitive 'moonlight' poets may be numerous, often melancholic, and sometimes die young; the 'sun-kindled' are constructive and rarer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical contest as social catharsis (boxing/self-defence)
rubrics_metrics.description: A bout with the gloves would let off the ill-nature, and cure the indigestion... A friendly contest in several rounds, at the close of which the parties shook hands and appeared cordially reconciled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Propose regulated physical contests (sparring, boxing) as a means to resolve quarrels, defuse rancor, and restore amicable relations; present as an alternative to extended public disputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of vice: find and remove the 'head' carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: What is the head of it, and where does it lie? The true way to deal with those obstinate animals... is to get a piece of silk round their heads, and pull them out very cautiously. If you only break them off, they grow worse than ever.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When addressing entrenched vices (addiction, intemperance), identify and attend to the root cause rather than apply superficial remedies that may worsen the condition; use careful, targeted intervention rather than blunt force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attitude toward aging: maintain inner cheerfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Call him not old, whose visionary brain Holds o'er the past its undivided reign... If yet the minstrel's song... Stir the few life-drops creeping round his heart,— Count his gray hairs,—they cannot make him old!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame aging as a condition determined more by inner vitality than by outward years; recommend cultivating cheerfulness, love, creativity, and active interest to retain youthfulness of spirit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effort and craft in producing distinctive poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: It is easy to grind out the song, but to plant these bristling points which make it was the painful task of time. Every note marks where a spur of steel has been driven in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize that originality and the memorable 'point' in poetry require deliberate, often painful labor; discourage reliance on facile repetition of familiar tunes—advocate craft, revision, and hard work to produce distinctive work.
